GasGas calls for **35 mm (1.38 in) static sag** and **105 mm (4.13 in) rider sag** on your 2023 MC 250F with stock rear suspension.

Measure from the rear axle to the SAG mark on the rear fender with the rear wheel hanging free. Subtract the same measurement with the bike upright under its own weight for static sag, then with you aboard in full gear, feet on the pegs, for rider sag. Set rider sag with preload first, then recheck static sag. If it’s well below 35 mm at 105 mm rider sag, the shock spring is likely too soft; well above 35 mm, it’s likely too stiff.

The U.S. front brake caliper recall lists the 2023–2025 GasGas MC 250F. Have a GasGas dealer confirm whether the recall work has been done on yours.
For your 2023 GasGas MC 250F with the stock shock and linkage, aim for 35 mm static sag and 105 mm rider sag.

**105 mm (4.1 in)** is Honda’s standard race sag for your 2022 CRF250R with the stock shock spring.

Measure from the center of the left rear fender bolt to the center of the chain adjuster locknut. Take one reading with the rear wheel off the ground, then another with you seated in full gear and fuel up to the bottom of the filler neck. Subtract the rider-on reading from the unloaded reading.

If you’re running a Honda optional shock spring, the targets are **110–115 mm** for the soft spring and **95–100 mm** for the stiff spring.

Honda calls for a fork oil change **every 9 races (about 22.5 riding hours)** and after the first break-in ride. For hard sand motos or lots of rough-track practice, 10–15 hours is a common shorter interval, not Honda’s schedule. If the fork starts bottoming more or the clickers stop making a noticeable difference, check it sooner.

For the stock springs, Honda specifies **5W fork fluid** and **380 cm³ (12.9 US fl oz) per leg** in the outer chamber. That’s the total volume, not what you pour in after a drain—some oil stays inside.

For your 2023 CRF450R, Honda offers one stiffer spring rate at each end:

- **Fork spring: 5.2 N/mm** (29.7 lbf/in), up from 5.0 N/mm (28.6 lbf/in) stock.
- **Shock spring: 58 N/mm** (331.2 lbf/in), up from 56 N/mm (319.8 lbf/in) stock.

You don’t have to change both ends together. If you fit the stiffer shock spring, reset rider sag and then check free sag before touching the clickers.

Don’t soften compression yet. A fork that rides too deep can feel sharp on small chop and still run out of travel on a landing.

With the fork cold and the front wheel off the ground, bleed the outer chambers—not the main air valve—and check the main pressure. GASGAS’s stock baseline is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**, with fork compression and rebound both **12 clicks out**. If pressure is low, bring it back to stock and retest first.

- **Fork air:** If it’s already at 10.4 bar and dives or uses lots of travel on ordinary hits, go from **10.4 to 10.6 bar (154 psi)** for more hold-up. Leave the clickers alone. Ride the same chop at the same pace; go back if it deflects more without gaining support.
- **Fork rebound:** If the first bump feels fine but the fork gets lower and harsher through the strip, test **12 to 13 clicks out** from stock instead. That lets it recover faster. Go back if the front starts springing back or wandering.

If it rides high and jars on the first small hit but still bottoms on landings, don’t keep adding air. Check for fork bind and check service history before chasing clickers.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork air pressure:** If the fork rides deep at the stock pressure, go from 10.4 to 10.6 bar cold.

**Fork compression:** If the air and sag check out, go 2 clicks firmer from where you are. If you're at the stock 12 clicks out, go **from 12 to 10 clicks out**. Leave rebound alone for this test.

Make three straight-line stops from the same marker at the same entry speed. Get your hips back over the pegs before you brake and squeeze the lever progressively. The fork should settle without dropping abruptly; go back two clicks if it starts skipping across braking bumps or loses front grip.

That sounds like **shock fade**: the rear compresses more easily and springs back faster once the damper heats up. Some change with temperature is normal; a clear loss of control isn’t. As an illustration, a typical 5W suspension oil is about 38% thinner at 95°F than at 60°F. That’s not a measurement of your shock, but it shows why a marginal damper can feel fine cold and go loose late in a moto.

With the bike off and cool, check the shock shaft and seal area for fresh oil. If the rear also **sits lower** after a moto—not just bounces more—Honda calls for checking for nitrogen loss. A dry shock can still have an internal problem. If it’s dry but the fade is repeatable, have a suspension shop check the nitrogen charge and compare damping cold and hot. Don’t add preload or slow the rebound to mask it, and don’t ride another moto to reproduce it if the rear is already hard to control.
Fine cold, then soft and bouncy after 20 minutes points to shock fade. Check for a leak before touching the clickers.

Leave the clickers alone and test one tire at a time, about **1 psi** from that baseline: try 14 psi for grip on smooth, slick dirt or deep sand, or 16 psi for rim protection on rocky, square-edged ground, within your tire’s limits. **The rear shock spring is likely too soft for you.** Your 105 mm (4.13 in) rider sag is right on GasGas’s target, but 20 mm static sag is 15 mm short of the 35 mm (1.38 in) target. A soft spring needs extra preload to hit 105 mm with you aboard, so the rear barely settles under the bike’s own weight.

Recheck static sag with the bike upright and no rider. Let the rear settle once after pushing it down and once after lifting it. If the readings differ noticeably, check for linkage or shock-bearing binding before buying a spring. If both are near 20 mm and you’re on the stock **42 N/mm shock spring**, try the next stiffer **45 N/mm shock spring**. Reset rider sag to 105 mm and check that static sag moves toward 35 mm. Leave the clickers alone for now.

On your 2023 CRF450R, **222.9 mm (8.78 in) is the shortest Honda allows** for the stock 56 N/mm shock spring. Measure the spring seat to seat with the bike on a stand and the rear wheel off the ground. Honda’s standard installed length is **232.3 mm (9.15 in)**, and the allowed range is 222.9–233 mm (8.78–9.20 in). Each full collar turn changes installed length by 1.5 mm and preload by 84 N, so the limit is 9.4 mm of additional spring compression from the standard setting—not 9.4 mm of total preload.

Set **105 mm race sag** in full gear first, then check free sag with the bike on its wheels and no rider. Honda doesn’t publish a free-sag target for this bike; **roughly 30–40 mm** is general guidance. If you have very little free sag at 105 mm, the spring is likely too soft even if the collar is still in range. If you can’t get down to 105 mm before the length limit, don’t crank it farther—Honda’s stiffer 58 N/mm shock spring is the next step.

If the spring has been swapped, Honda’s installed-length ranges differ: **224.1–233 mm** for the soft 54 N/mm shock spring and **223.7–233 mm** for the stiff 58 N/mm shock spring.
On the stock 56 N/mm shock spring, an installed length shorter than 222.9 mm (8.78 in) is too much preload. If you reach that limit and still have more than 105 mm of race sag, go to a stiffer spring.

The difference is what holds the front end up: **trapped air in an air fork, a steel coil in a spring fork**. Both still use oil damping to control how fast the fork moves.

On your 2023 MC 250F’s stock WP XACT AER, the **left leg houses the air spring**. A sealed piston squeezes the air as the fork compresses, so the spring gets progressively firmer deeper in the stroke. A balance chamber helps the fork start moving smoothly near full extension. The **right leg houses the oil damping cartridge**, where the compression and rebound adjusters control oil flow. GasGas’s standard spring pressure is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**, checked cold with the front wheel off the ground.

A coil fork gets its support from a steel spring in one or both legs, depending on the design. A straight-rate coil adds roughly the same amount of force for each extra inch of travel, though trapped air above the fork oil adds some progression near the end. To change the spring rate, you swap coils instead of adjusting air pressure. The clickers change damping, not spring rate, on either fork.
An air fork uses compressed air instead of a steel coil to hold the bike up. Both designs use oil to control how fast the fork compresses and returns.

A **compression test** reads peak pressure in psi while the starter spins your 450 SX-F. A low reading tells you it isn’t building much pressure, but it doesn’t tell you why. Cranking speed, valve timing and the automatic decompressor can all affect the reading.

A **leak-down test** feeds regulated shop air through the spark-plug hole with the piston at top dead center on the compression stroke, both valves closed and the crank held securely. The tester shows a leakage percentage, and where the air escapes tells you what to check:

- **Throttle body:** intake valve isn’t sealing.
- **Muffler:** exhaust valve isn’t sealing.
- **Crankcase breather:** air is getting past the rings; a little is normal.
- **Bubbles in the coolant during the test:** suspect a head-gasket leak or a crack into the cooling jacket.

If you’re deciding whether to look at the head or the piston and cylinder, leak-down is the more useful test. It shows the leak path, not the exact failed part.
A compression test tells you how much pressure the engine builds while cranking. A leak-down test tells you how well the cylinder seals and helps pinpoint where it leaks.

Squish is the **gap between the piston crown and the flat or angled band around the edge of the cylinder head** when the piston is at the very top of its travel. As the piston comes up, it squeezes the fuel-air mix out of that narrow gap toward the center of the chamber. That movement creates turbulence, which helps the mixture burn faster and more evenly.

Too wide and you lose much of that effect. Too tight and the piston can touch the head at high rpm or as carbon builds up. Tightening the gap can also raise compression if chamber volume isn't corrected, so builders check both rather than chasing the smallest gap.

On your 2022 YZ125, the exact factory squish figure isn't confirmed here. A builder measures the actual gap with soft solder at opposite sides of the bore with the head torqued down. That's a different measurement from piston-to-cylinder clearance, which is the gap between the piston skirt and the cylinder wall.
Squish is the gap between the piston crown and the outer band of the cylinder head at top dead center. Builders set it to improve combustion while leaving enough clearance to keep the piston from touching the head.

Use **Setup Log** in BAK MX, or a pocket notebook if you prefer paper. Keep one baseline page and one short entry per test. The key is writing down **what you went from and to**, not just “went softer.”

**Baseline:** Record what’s actually on the bike: fork and shock springs, rider and free sag, fork height, clickers, and cold tire pressures. If the suspension is stock, Honda’s reference for your 2022 CRF250R is fork spring **4.8 N/mm**, shock spring **50 N/mm**, and **105 mm rider sag**. Fork compression/rebound are **12/13 clicks out**; shock low-speed compression/rebound are **6/11 clicks out**, and high-speed compression is **2 1/6 turns out**. Count from lightly seated. Honda doesn’t publish a free-sag target for this bike; log what you measure with the bike on its wheels and no rider.

**Copy this for each test:** `Date / track | dirt + conditions | symptom + where | setting before → after | better / worse / no change | keep / revert`

Example: `Dry hardpack | fork deflects on corner entry | fork comp 12 → 13 out | tracks better, no extra dive | keep.` Change one thing, then ride the same section at the same pace for a few laps.

**Suspension setup makes the biggest difference.** Testers consistently found the 2023 chassis stiff over braking bumps. Get the fork and shock working together before spending money on bars, clamps, or a coil kit.

1. **Set sag and fork air first.** With stock suspension, KTM’s targets are **105 mm rider sag** in full gear and **35 mm static sag** with no rider. KTM lists shock springs of 42 N/mm for 143–165 lb, 45 N/mm for 165–187 lb, and 48 N/mm for 187–209 lb. If static sag comes out well below 35 mm once rider sag is set, the shock spring is too soft. The stock WP air fork uses pressure, not a coil rate: start at **10.7 bar (155 psi)** cold with the front wheel off the ground.
2. **Fit the controls before replacing them.** Set the lever reach and angle so you can cover the brake and clutch while standing without bending your wrists or squeezing the grips harder.
3. **Make the 450 easier to ride late in a moto.** Try the milder map on slick dirt and short-shift where the bike still pulls cleanly. If the fork still deflects off small braking bumps after setup, I’d spend on valving for your weight and pace before buying a coil conversion.
For vet comfort on the 2023 KTM 450 SX-F, get the suspension balanced for your weight first. Then fit the controls to your hands and calm the power delivery before buying parts.
